claim: Acinetobacter baumannii is a Gram-negative bacterial pathogen that causes a wide variety of nosocomial infections.
source: Acinetobacter baumannii is a Gram-negative bacterial pathogen that causes a wide variety of nosocomial infections (Wong et al., 2017; Piperaki et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wong et al., 2017 and Piperaki et al., 2019

claim: Acinetobacter baumannii causes urinary tract infections, gastrointestinal and skin/wound infections, and secondary meningitis.
source: including urinary tract infections, gastrointestinal and skin/wound infections, and secondary meningitis (Peleg et al., 2008; Nasr, 2020; Doi et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Peleg et al., 2008; Nasr, 2020; and Doi et al., 2015

claim: Isolates of Acinetobacter baumannii have emerged that are resistant to almost all available antibiotics, including colistin, tigecycline, and carbapenems.
source: The challenge posed by this pathogen is compounded by the emergence of isolates that are resistant to almost all of the available antibiotics, including some of the last resort for treatment of infections caused by bacterial pathogens, including colistin, tigecycline, and carbapenems (Piperaki et al., 2019; Karakonstantis, 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Piperaki et al., 2019 and Karakonstantis, 2021

claim: The World Health Organization has classified A. baumannii as a pathogen for which new antibiotics are urgently needed.
source: As a result, the World Health Organization (WHO) has classified A. baumannii as a pathogen for which new antibiotics are urgently needed (Whiteway et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Whiteway et al., 2022

claim: The majority of clinically used antibiotic classes originate from soil bacteria, including lactams, aminoglycosides, polymyxins, and glycopeptides.
source: The majority of clinically used antibiotic classes originate from soil bacteria, including lactams, aminoglycosides, polymyxins, and glycopeptides (Hutchings et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hutchings et al., 2019

claim: There has not been a novel antibiotic discovered in over 30 years using traditional methods of screening environmental samples.
source: As a result, there has not been a novel antibiotic discovered in over 30 years using traditional methods of screening environmental samples (Lewis, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lewis, 2020

claim: Wang et al. identified 453 candidate essential genes for the growth of A. baumannii strain ATCC 17978 on rich medium using In-seq.
source: Using In-seq Wang et al. identified 453 candidate essential genes for the growth of A. baumannii strain ATCC 17978 on rich medium (Wang et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2014

claim: From 10 genes examined, three were found to be essential for A. baumannii viability on rich medium.
source: From 10 genes examined, three were found to be essential for A. baumannii viability on rich medium.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A1S_0137, A1S_2249, and A1S_3387 are required for growth on Luria Bertani agar.
source: Our initial analysis of 10 genes (Supplementary file 1) identified A1S_0137, A1S_2249, and A1S_3387 (Smith et al., 2007) that met the criteria of being required for growth on Luria Bertani (LB) agar (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Gene A1S_3387 is essential for A. baumannii growth in the Vogel–Bonner minimal medium with succinate as the sole carbon source.
source: Importantly, gene A1S_3387 is also essential for A. baumannii growth in the Vogel–Bonner minimal medium with succinate (VBS) as the sole carbon source (Vogel and Bonner, 1956; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Vogel and Bonner, 1956

claim: Aeg1 has orthologs in a number of Gram-negative bacteria, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Salmonella enterica, members of the Moraxellaceae family and some strains of Escherichia coli, with sequence similarity ranging from 80% to identical.
source: Sequence analysis revealed that Aeg1 has orthologs in a number of Gram-negative bacteria, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Salmonella enterica members of the Moraxellaceae family and some strains of Escherichia coli, with sequence similarity ranging from 80% to identical (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Aeg1 is predicted to harbor a single transmembrane domain.
source: Aeg1 is predicted to harbor a single transmembrane domain, however, the precise location of this transmembrane segment has been predicted differently across various analyses.
evidence: The claim is based on computational predictions using bioinformatics tools

claim: Expression of the Aeg1 mutant lacking N-terminal region was unable to restore the growth of the strain.
source: Importantly, expression of the Aeg1 mutant lacking N-terminal region was unable to restore the growth of the strain (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The N-terminal domain of Aeg1 is essential for its activity.
source: suggesting that N-terminal domain of Aeg1 is essential for its activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that the N-terminal deletion mutant cannot complement the growth defect

claim: Depletion of Aeg1 causes cell elongation in A. baumannii.
source: These results indicate that depletion of Aeg1 causes cell elongation, a phenotype that had been observed in recent studies using transposon insertion sequencing (Bai et al., 2021; Pichoff et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations to Bai et al., 2021 and Pichoff et al., 2012

claim: In medium without ara, more than 96% of the cells of strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) become elongated with cell lengths ranging from 5 μm to over 10 μm after 18 hr incubation.
source: Incubation in medium without ara for 18 hr caused more than 96% of the cells to become elongated with cell lengths ranging from 5 μm to over 10 μm (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The cell elongation phenotype caused by Aeg1 depletion can be partially reversed after growing the elongated cells in medium containing 1% ara for 4 hr.
source: The phenotype can be partially reversed after growing the elongated cells in medium containing 1% ara for 4 hr (Figure 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Two suppressor mutants M1 and M2 derived from strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) were able to grow on medium without ara at rates comparable to those of wild-type bacteria.
source: In spotting assays using diluted cells, each of these two mutants derived from strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) was able to grow on medium without ara at rates comparable to those of wild-type bacteria (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Mutant M1 had 320 substitution mutations and 659 insertion–deletion mutations.
source: We then performed whole-genome sequencing analysis of these two mutants, which revealed that M1 and M2 had 320 and 328 substitution mutations, respectively. In addition, 659 insertion–deletion (InDel) mutations were found in M1 and 665 such mutations were associated with M2 (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data

claim: Mutant M2 had 328 substitution mutations and 665 insertion–deletion mutations.
source: We then performed whole-genome sequencing analysis of these two mutants, which revealed that M1 and M2 had 320 and 328 substitution mutations, respectively. In addition, 659 insertion–deletion (InDel) mutations were found in M1 and 665 such mutations were associated with M2 (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data

claim: An E202K mutation in the cell division protein FtsA was found in both suppressor mutants M1 and M2.
source: An E202K mutation caused by a G to A substitution in the first position of the codon was found in the cell division protein FtsA in both M1 and M2 (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data

claim: Expression of FtsAE202K allowed strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) to gain the ability to grow in the absence of ara.
source: Expression of FtsAE202K allowed strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) to gain the ability to grow in the absence of ara.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: FtsA cannot suppress the growth defect caused by Aeg1 depletion despite being expressed at a comparable level to FtsAE202K.
source: In contrast, although the protein was expressed at a comparable level, FtsA cannot suppress the growth defect caused by Aeg1 depletion (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Expression of FtsAE202K in strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) under conditions in which the complementation gene was not expressed displayed a morphology similar to that of wild-type bacteria.
source: Consistent with the growth phenotypes, expression of FtsAE202K in strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) under conditions in which the complementation gene was not expressed displayed a morphology similar to that of wild-type bacteria (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: FtsAR286W (FtsA*) was the first gain-of-function mutation found in E. coli, which allowed the survival of mutants lacking ZipA or FtsK.
source: Among these, FtsAR286W (FtsA*) was the first gain-of-function mutation found in E. coli, which allowed the survival of mutants lacking ZipA (ΔzipA) or FtsK (ΔftsK) (Berezuk et al., 2020; Bernard et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berezuk et al., 2020; Bernard et al., 2007; and Liu et al., 2015

claim: FtsAI143L and FtsAE124A weakly bypassed the requirement of FtsN in E. coli.
source: Additionally, FtsAI143L(Park et al., 2021) and FtsAE124A(Geissler et al., 2003) weakly bypassed the requirement of FtsN.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2021 and Geissler et al., 2003

claim: Expression of FtsAD124A or FtsAV144L partially rescued the growth of strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) in medium without ara.
source: Whereas FtsAQ285W cannot detectably suppress Aeg1 depletion, expression of FtsAD124A or FtsAV144L partially resecured the growth of strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) in medium without ara (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: FtsAQ285W cannot detectably suppress Aeg1 depletion.
source: Whereas FtsAQ285W cannot detectably suppress Aeg1 depletion, expression of FtsAD124A or FtsAV144L partially resecured the growth of strain ∆aeg1(PBAD::Aeg1) in medium without ara (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Aeg1 localized at the septum of dividing cells.
source: Fluorescence microscopy analysis revealed that Aeg1 localized at the septum of dividing cells (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Aeg1 interacts with ZipA, FtsK, FtsL, FtsB, and FtsN.
source: Among the tested proteins FtsZ, FtsA, ZipA, FtsK, FtsQ, FtsL, FtsB, FtsW, FtsI, and FtsN, Aeg1 detectably interacts with ZipA, FtsK, FtsL, FtsB, and FtsN.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 4A-D

claim: ZipA and FtsN have higher binding affinity with Aeg1 whether the T25 reporter domain was fused to the N- or C-terminus of the Aeg1 construct.
source: Intriguingly, ZipA and FtsN appearing to have higher binding affinity with Aeg1 whether the T25 reporter domain was fused to the N- or C-terminus of the Aeg1 construct (Figure 4A–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 4A-D

claim: Aeg1 colocalized with ZipA, FtsL, FtsB, and FtsN.
source: Consistent with results from the protein interaction experiments using the bacterial two-hybrid assay, we found that Aeg1 colocalized with ZipA, FtsL, FtsB, and FtsN (Figure 4E, red arrows)
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4E

claim: In cells depleted of Aeg1, all of the examined core division proteins displayed midcell mistargeting, including ZipA, FtsB, FtsL, and FtsN.
source: In cells depleted of Aeg1, all of the examined core division proteins displayed midcell mistargeting, including ZipA, FtsB, FtsL, and FtsN (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Aeg1 is a new member of cell division protein, which plays a role in positioning several other core proteins at the septum of A. baumannii.
source: These results suggest that Aeg1 is a new member of cell division protein, which plays a role in positioning several other core proteins at the septum of A. baumannii.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that Aeg1 depletion causes mislocalization of core division proteins

claim: Induction of HA-FtsBE65A completely restored the growth of the Δaeg1 mutant in the absence of Aeg1.
source: Although the expression of HA-FtsBE65A was not detectable with the HA-specific antibody, induction of this mutant completely restored the growth of the Δaeg1 mutant in the absence of Aeg1 (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: HA-FtsBD68H cannot bypass the requirement of Aeg1.
source: In contrast, a similarly constructed plasmid that directs the expression of HA-FtsBD68H cannot bypass the requirement of Aeg1 under the same conditions (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Expressed HA-FtsLQ70K detectably rescued bacterial growth without Aeg1 at a level considerably lower than that of FtsBE65A.
source: Similarly, expressed HA-FtsLQ70K detectably rescued bacterial growth without Aeg1 at a level considerably lower than that of FtsBE65A (Figure 5C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Overexpression of FtsWM254I and FtsWS274G of A. baumannii detectably rescued the growth of the strain in which Aeg1 had been depleted.
source: Overexpression of FtsWM254I and FtsWS274G of A. baumannii detectably rescued the growth of the strain in which Aeg1 had been depleted (Figure 5D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Aeg1 may collaborate with FtsN to activate at least a part of FtsQLB and FtsA for subsequently activation of FtsWI during cell division.
source: Therefore, our results demonstrate that Aeg1 may collaborate with FtsN to activate at least a part of FtsQLB and FtsA for subsequently activation of FtsWI during cell division.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations that constitutively active mutants of FtsQLB, FtsA, and FtsW can bypass the requirement of Aeg1

claim: The Aeg1–FtsN complex is involved in the activation of FtsQLB and FtsA.
source: Together with results that the variant FtsAE202K suppressed the growth defect caused by aeg1 depletion (Figure 3B), these observations support a model in which the Aeg1–FtsN complex is involved in the activation of FtsQLB and FtsA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations including suppression by FtsAE202K and constitutively active mutants of FtsQLB

claim: From 10 putative essential genes identified by In-seq, three previously annotated as hypotheticals are essential for A. baumannii viability.
source: Using a conditional gene deletion method, we have revealed that from 10 putative essential genes identified by this method, three previously annotated as hypotheticals are essential for A. baumannii viability
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from conditional gene deletion experiments

claim: Assignment of essentiality to genes identified by In-seq methods needs to be individually verified.
source: suggesting that assignment of essentiality to genes identified by methods of this kind needs to be individually verified.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only 3 out of 10 tested genes were confirmed to be essential

claim: The assignment of aeg1 as an essential gene is consistent with a recent study which revealed its essentiality (termed advA) by transposon insertion sequencing.
source: Our assignment of aeg1 as an essential gene is consistent with a recent study which revealed its essentiality (termed advA) by transposon insertion sequencing, which also observed cell elongation upon the depletion of this gene (Pichoff et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pichoff et al., 2012

claim: Over 30 distinct proteins are assembled into the bacterial divisome.
source: In the process of bacterial cell division, over 30 distinct proteins are assembled into a complex typically referred to as 'divisome' (Haeusser and Margolin, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Haeusser and Margolin, 2016

claim: Ten proteins are normally essential for both cell division and survival, and they are now mainly suggested to be the core of the divisome in various bacteria.
source: Ten of these are normally essential for both cell division and survival, and they are now mainly suggested to be the core of the divisome in various bacteria (Haeusser and Margolin, 2016; Lutkenhaus, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haeusser and Margolin, 2016 and Lutkenhaus, 2017

claim: The FtsQLB complex serves as a scaffold for recruitment of subsequent divisome proteins.
source: Among these, the FtsQLB complex not only serves as a scaffold for recruitment of subsequent divisome proteins (Guzman et al., 1997; Craven et al., 2024)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guzman et al., 1997 and Craven et al., 2024

claim: The FtsQLB complex plays an important role in regulating the activity of the divisome.
source: Among these, the FtsQLB complex not only serves as a scaffold for recruitment of subsequent divisome proteins (Guzman et al., 1997; Craven et al., 2024), but also plays an important role in regulating the activity of the divisome (Park et al., 2021; Park et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2021 and Park et al., 2020

claim: The constriction control domain (CCD) of FtsL is a critical component for switching the conformation of FtsLB from an off to an on state in order to activate FtsWI.
source: The constriction control domain (CCD) of FtsL was previously defined as a critical component for switching the conformation of FtsLB from an off to an on state in order to activate FtsWI by enabling the interaction between FtsIperi and the AWI (activation of FtsWI) region of FtsL (Park et al., 2021; Park et al., 2020; Sánchez et al., 1994)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2021; Park et al., 2020; and Sánchez et al., 1994

claim: Aeg1 functions upstream of FtsB and FtsW.
source: Division obstruction caused by Aeg1 depletion can be effectively circumvented by suppression mutations (FtsBE65A) in its CCD domain and by activation mutations (M254I and S274G) of FtsW (Figure 5D), suggesting that Aeg1 functions upstream of these proteins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that constitutively active mutants of FtsB and FtsW can bypass the requirement of Aeg1

claim: The constitutively active form of FtsA (FtsA*) acts on FtsW in the cytoplasm.
source: In addition to FtsQLB-mediated activation of FtsI in the periplasm, the constitutively active form of FtsA (FtsA*) acting on FtsW in the cytoplasm, these two events functions synergistically to activate FtsWI for sPG synthesis (Karimova et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karimova et al., 1998

claim: FtsA is a member of the actin family.
source: FtsA is a member of the actin family (van den Ent and Löwe, 2000; Szwedziak et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to van den Ent and Löwe, 2000 and Szwedziak et al., 2012

claim: FtsA interacts with FtsN via a unique IC domain positioned between the IA and IIA domains.
source: which interacts with FtsN via a unique IC domain positioned between the IA and IIA domains (Baranova et al., 2020; Pichoff et al., 2015; Goehring and Beckwith, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baranova et al., 2020; Pichoff et al., 2015; and Goehring and Beckwith, 2005

claim: The E202K mutation in the IIA domain of FtsA bypasses the requirement of Aeg1 by A. baumannii.
source: That the E202K mutation in the IIA domain bypasses the requirement of Aeg1 by A. baumannii (Figure 3B) suggests that Aeg1 and FtsA work together to activate FtsW.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Aeg1 and FtsA work together to activate FtsW.
source: That the E202K mutation in the IIA domain bypasses the requirement of Aeg1 by A. baumannii (Figure 3B) suggests that Aeg1 and FtsA work together to activate FtsW.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the FtsAE202K mutation can bypass the requirement of Aeg1

claim: The maturation of the core divisome is facilitated by the recruitment in a nearly sequential order of the late-division proteins FtsK, FtsQ, FtsL/FtsB, FtsW, FtsI, and FtsN.
source: The maturation of the core divisome is facilitated by the recruitment in a nearly sequential order of the late-division proteins FtsK, FtsQ, FtsL/FtsB, FtsW, FtsI, and FtsN (Du et al., 2019; Addinall et al., 1997; Lyu et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2019; Addinall et al., 1997; and Lyu et al., 2022

claim: Once FtsN is recruited, division-specific peptidoglycan synthesis conferred by the FtsWI complex is activated to build the septum.
source: Once the latest division protein, FtsN, is recruited, division-specific peptidoglycan synthesis conferred by the FtsWI complex is activated to build the septum (Lyu et al., 2022; Weiss, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lyu et al., 2022 and Weiss, 2015

claim: By binding to FtsA, a small amount of FtsN is recruited to the division site earlier than previously thought.
source: More recent studies suggest that by binding to FtsA, a small amount of FtsN is recruited to the division site earlier than previously thought (Park et al., 2021; Goehring and Beckwith, 2005; Piehaud and Second, 1951)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2021; Goehring and Beckwith, 2005; and Piehaud and Second, 1951

claim: FtsN induces a conformational switch in both FtsA and the FtsQLB subcomplex on both sides of the membrane.
source: More recent studies suggest that by binding to FtsA, a small amount of FtsN is recruited to the division site earlier than previously thought (Park et al., 2021; Goehring and Beckwith, 2005; Piehaud and Second, 1951) where it induces a conformational switch in both FtsA and the FtsQLB subcomplex on both sides of the membrane (Park et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2021

claim: Binding between FtsA and FtsN is regulated by ZipA.
source: Furthermore, binding between FtsA and FtsN is regulated by ZipA (Goehring and Beckwith, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goehring and Beckwith, 2005

claim: Aeg1 participates in cell division by anchoring to the division site together with ZipA where it recruits FtsN, which in turn signals to both the cytoplasmic and periplasmic branches of peptidoglycan synthesis involving FtsA and the FtsQLB complex, respectively.
source: Our observation of strong binding of Aeg1 to ZipA and FtsN (Figure 4A–D) prompted us to propose a model in which Aeg1 participates in cell division by anchoring to the division site together with ZipA where it recruits FtsN, which in turn signals to both the cytoplasmic and periplasmic branches of peptidoglycan synthesis involving FtsA and the FtsQLB complex, respectively (Park et al., 2021; Figure 6A)
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental observations of protein interactions and suppression by constitutively active mutants

claim: Aeg1 is one of the early arrivals in the hierarchical sequential assembly of the divisome.
source: The placement of Aeg1 as one of the early arrivals in the hierarchical sequential assembly of the divisome is consistent with the fact that the requirement of Aeg1 can be bypassed by constitutively active mutants of FtsAE202K (Figure 3), FtsB (FtsBE65A), FtsL (FtsLQ70K), and of FtsW (FtsWM254I and FtsWS274G) (Figure 5)
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that constitutively active mutants of downstream proteins can bypass the requirement of Aeg1

claim: Homologs of Aeg1 are present in many Gram-negative bacteria, including some recent isolate of E. coli.
source: It is worth noting that that although homologs of Aeg1 are present in many Gram-negative bacteria, including some recent isolate of E. coli, it appears to be absent in more extensively studied model strains such as K12 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Aeg1 appears to be absent in E. coli K12.
source: It is worth noting that that although homologs of Aeg1 are present in many Gram-negative bacteria, including some recent isolate of E. coli, it appears to be absent in more extensively studied model strains such as K12 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: In E. coli K12, the activity of Aeg1 may be conferred by a yet unidentified protein that employs a conserved mechanism in cell division.
source: It is possible that in strain K12, its activity is conferred by a yet unidentified protein that employs a conserved mechanism in cell division.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about how E. coli K12 might compensate for the absence of Aeg1

claim: Aeg1 interacts with multiple cell division proteins, including FtsN, which is required for components of the divisome to localize to the midcell.
source: Our results reveal that the protein, termed Aeg1 interacts with multiple cell division proteins, including FtsN, which is required for components of the divisome to localize to the midcell.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial two-hybrid and colocalization data presented in the manuscript

claim: The FtsAE202K and FtsBE65A mutants effectively bypassed the need of Aeg1 by A. baumannii.
source: We demonstrate that the FtsAE202K and FtsBE65A mutants effectively bypassed the need of Aeg1 by A. baumannii
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 5B

claim: The activation variants FtsWM254I and FtsWS274G bypassed the need of Aeg1 by A. baumannii.
source: as did the activation variants FtsWM254I and FtsWS274G.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Aeg1 is a cell division protein that arrives at the division site to initiate cell division by recruiting FtsN, which activates FtsQLB and FtsA to induce the septal peptidoglycan synthase FtsWI.
source: Our results suggest that Aeg1 is a cell division protein that arrives at the division site to initiate cell division by recruiting FtsN, which activates FtsQLB and FtsA to induce the septal peptidoglycan synthase FtsWI.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on multiple experimental observations including protein interactions, localization, and suppression by constitutively active mutants

claim: The discovery of the new essential cell division protein has provided a new target for the development of antibacterial agents.
source: The discovery of the new essential cell division protein has provided a new target for the development of antibacterial agents.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential application of the discovery

claim: All A. baumannii strains used in this study were derivatives of strain ATCC17978.
source: All A. baumannii strains were derivatives of strain ATCC17978 (Yildirim et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is a statement about the materials used in the study, supported by a citation to Yildirim et al., 2016

claim: Removal of arabinose for 6 hr rendered Aeg1-mCherry undetectable in approximately 90% of the cells.
source: Importantly, we found that removal of arabinose for 6 hr rendered Aeg1-mCherry undetectable in approximately 90% of the cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Expression of mutants FtsIK211I, FtsWM269I, and FtsWE289G driven by a strong promoter can bypass the need of FtsN in E. coli.
source: It is known that expression of mutants FtsIK211I, FtsWM269I, and FtsWE289G driven by a strong promoter can bypass the need of FtsN in E. coli (de Boer, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Boer, 2010

claim: FtsI from A. baumannii does not have a residue corresponding to K211 of its E. coli counterpart.
source: FtsI from A. baumannii does not have a residue corresponding to K211 of its E. coli counterpart (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2
